A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Rec-R1 research. Their full text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices A–G support comparison. Internal reporting inconsistencies in v3 do not prevent identifying the changes.

before.justification: v2 reports original product-search and sequential-recommendation experiments, prompt and SFT-format analyses, generalization evaluations, and qualitative cases.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds re-ranking, alternative-backbone, baseline-comparison, standard retrieval, and multi-objective reward experiments.

M1.justification: v3 implements closed-set re-ranking using query-plus-candidate inputs and ordered item-ID outputs. Appendix E.7 also adds a composite reward combining NDCG, output format, and category consistency. These extend the retained GRPO framework without replacing its core optimization procedure.

E1.justification: v3 adds product re-ranking on ESCI, a distinct task requiring ordering supplied candidates. Appendix E.5 adds MS MARCO, NFCorpus, FEVER, and TREC DL’19/DL’20 retrieval evaluations. The earlier product-search, Amazon Beauty, and general-capability benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: New evaluated comparators include rejection-sampling fine-tuning and DPO; DocT5Query, RetPO, LLM4CS, and AdaQR; and Search-R1 and ConvSearch-R1. The new re-ranking comparison includes Qwen3-Reranker-4B/8B, GPT-4o, and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct. Original comparison sets are retained.

E3.justification: New re-ranking settings use shared top-16 candidates, exclude zero-NDCG@20 retrieval cases, use 2,166/521/465 train/validation/test samples, and evaluate NDCG@10. Additional experiments vary backbone size/family, specify rejection-sampling and DPO procedures, and introduce MRR@10/NDCG@10 retrieval evaluations. The original training recipe remains; removal of ESCI’s 'per category' qualifier does not clearly establish a changed split.

E4.justification: v3 adds tests of sensitivity to backbone size and family, comparisons of alternative fine-tuning strategies, and a multi-objective reward analysis (Tables 9, 10, and 20). These examine additional questions about generality and optimization. Earlier prompt-style ablations, SFT-format analyses, and both case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or result error bars. Both already specify 12 sampled responses per prompt for GRPO; these are rollouts rather than uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Original Tables 1–3 and the matched prompt/forgetting tables retain their values. v3 adds substantial re-ranking, backbone, baseline, retrieval, and multi-reward results. Table 4 shows Rec-R1 winning three domains but trailing GPT-4o in Video Games, 53.04 versus 61.57. New Tables 12 and 19 label Amazon-C4 comparisons as BM25 but repeat Table 2’s BLAIR-Large scores, 26.51/27.04/23.10/27.40, leaving those comparisons internally inconsistent.

T1.justification: The original SFT theorem and proof survive as Fact 1. New Appendices C.2–C.3 add a bounded-reward performance-gap bound in terms of expected KL divergence, proved using total variation, Pinsker, and Jensen inequalities, and an RL-over-SFT dominance theorem assuming global reward maximization within the same policy class.

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions expand empirical validation from two tasks to three and add a re-ranking superiority claim. Appendix A changes closed-set generation from future work to demonstrated coverage of all four paradigms. The central closed-loop optimization, avoidance of distilled supervision, and capability-preservation claims remain.

C2.justification: New passages attribute DPO’s weakness to static preference supervision, contrast large-cutoff metric rewards with ConvSearch-R1’s reward design, and interpret multi-reward results as evidence of flexibility. Existing explanations of transductive weaknesses, prompt-guided exploration, forgetting, and static-log versus live feedback remain substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 adds the re-ranking prompt, candidate construction and filtering instructions, split counts, and 3000/1024-token input/output limits. It also documents rejection-sampling and DPO data construction. Earlier VeRL, GPU, retriever, and training hyperparameter disclosures remain, without a new implementation-access statement.

R1.justification: New Appendix B.3 substantially expands positioning against LLM query rewriting, while E.6 distinguishes Rec-R1 from Search-R1 and ConvSearch-R1 through reward design and reported comparisons. Additional citations cover modern rewriting methods, Qwen3 rerankers, standard retrieval benchmarks, and trust-region theory; the earlier related-work discussion is retained.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the overall narrative remain. Local revisions update the introduction and Appendix A, rename Theorem 1 as Fact 1, consolidate prompt text, and change affiliations and publication headers. New scientific subsections expand the outline without a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: Journal reformatting changes typography, text width, author layout, table-caption placement, and prompt displays. Ten tables are added. The taxonomy moves from v2 Figure 4 in Appendix A to v3 Figure 1 in the introduction; existing plots and case-study figures are retained, relocated, or enlarged.

improvement.justification: Compared with v2, the re-ranking experiment, backbone/reward checks, and closer baselines provide useful additional support for Rec-R1’s generality. However, the inconsistent Amazon-C4 BM25 rows in Tables 12 and 19 weaken the new comparisons, and the re-ranking prose overstates Table 4, where GPT-4o wins Video Games. These reporting problems limit the net benefit of the expanded evidence.
